items.stem: Reducing the step size in an Euler integration of an ODE generally reduces truncation error but

options.text: increases accumulated round-off error and run time, so there is an optimal step size
options.rationale: Correct: smaller steps reduce truncation error but accumulate more round-off and cost; an optimum exists.
Floating-point and accumulated error prevent exactness.
Step size directly affects truncation error.
Stability depends on the method and problem, not step size alone.

items.stem: Which TWO practices help ensure a physics simulation's results are trustworthy? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Comparing output against an analytic solution in a limiting case
options.rationale: Correct: validation against a known limit builds trust.

options.text: Checking that a conserved quantity such as energy stays bounded
options.rationale: Correct: monitoring conserved quantities reveals integration errors.

options.text: Choosing the step size that produces the prettiest plot
options.rationale: Visual appeal is not a correctness criterion.

options.text: Running only once with default settings
options.rationale: Convergence and sensitivity checks require varying parameters.

items.explanation: Correct: validation against a known limit builds trust.

items.stem: A fourth-order Runge-Kutta method is often preferred over the Euler method for the same step size because it

options.text: achieves much smaller truncation error per step for a modest extra cost
options.rationale: Correct: RK4 has higher-order accuracy, greatly reducing error for a small cost increase.
RK4 can still be unstable for stiff problems or large steps.
RK4 uses several evaluations per step.
Round-off error is independent of the integration order.

items.explanation: Correct: RK4 has higher-order accuracy, greatly reducing error for a small cost increase.
